text:
The young men are smiling,

the old men are rejoicing

because, companions, they say

there is liberty for the people.


The throng is all song,

the bell towers, clamor,

the balconies, lights,

and the little squares, festivities.


A great novelty in the laws,

which, I swear, I do not understand,

happens when we see men

in such jubilation.


Many blessings, the learned say,

are preparing for the kingdom;

if men gain by it,

I rejoice for the men;


But for us women,

I neither praise it nor feel it,

for though laws may change

there are no rights for us.


Liberty! What does it matter to us?

What do we gain, what shall we have?

A prison as a tribune

and a needle as a right?


Liberty! What use is it to us

if our tyrants are

not the yoke of monarchs,

but the yoke of our sex?


Liberty! Is it not a bloody

sarcasm they make of us

by repeating that cry

before our irons?


Liberty! Ah, for weeping

we had it in every age;

with despots we wept,

with taxes we shall weep;


For these men, humane

and generous, like those others,

are ready in every century

to sanction our pains.


The young men are proud,

the old men are rejoicing,

equality is in the homeland,

liberty in the kingdom.


But I tell you, companions,

that the law is theirs alone,

that women are not counted

nor is there a Nation for this sex.


Therefore, though I hear them,

I neither applaud nor feel it;

if they lose, God repay them!

and if they win, good for them!

translation.title: Liberty
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The 1846 date footer is omitted as bibliographic matter; the poem’s feminist irony and refrain remain.
